title: Check your understanding: Reverting a Commit

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of reverting a commit?
options: `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses the change introduced by an earlier commit when that reversal applies. It is often suitable for shared history because it does not move an existing public branch backward.
Git automatically backs up every file, including ignored and untracked files, to a remote.
The operation grants every contributor write access to the hosted repository.
questions.answer_key: `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses the change introduced by an earlier commit when that reversal applies. It is often suitable for shared history because it does not move an existing public branch backward.
questions.explanation: `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses the change introduced by an earlier commit when that reversal applies. It is often suitable for shared history because it does not move an existing public branch backward.

questions.prompt: Which command is the most direct starting point for this lesson’s example?
questions.explanation: Use `git revert --no-edit <commit-id>` as the first inspection/action in the example, and then verify the result with the companion checks in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest general practice when working with reverting a commit?
options: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
Run the most destructive option first; the reflog guarantees every file can always be recovered.
Assume the local command also changed the remote and satisfied all hosting-platform policies.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
questions.explanation: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
